nodes.name: Gauss measure
nodes.statement: Denote by $\gamma$ the Gauss measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, i.e., the probability measure with density $\gamma_0(x)=\pi^{-n/2}\, \mathrm{e}^{-\mod{x}^2}$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\lambda$.
differentia: with density $\gamma_0(x)=\pi^{-n/2}\, \mathrm{e}^{-\mod{x}^2}$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\lambda$

nodes.name: Euclidean distance d
nodes.statement: Harmonic analysis on the measured metric space $(\mathbb{R}^n,d,\gamma)$, where $d$ denotes the Euclidean distance on $\mathbb{R}^n$, has been the object of many investigations.

nodes.name: Admissible ball at scale s
nodes.statement: A closed Euclidean ball $B$ is called \emph{admissible} at scale $s>0$ if $$ r_B \leq s\ \min\bigl(1,1/\mod{c_B}\bigr); $$ here and in the sequel $r_B$ and $c_B$ denote the radius and the centre of $B$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: A ball is admissible at scale s if its radius is at most s min(1, 1/|centre|).

nodes.name: Family B_s of admissible balls
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{B}_s$ the family of all balls admissible at scale $s$.

nodes.name: Admissible balls
nodes.statement: For the sake of brevity, we shall refer to balls in $\mathcal{B}_1$ simply as admissible balls.

nodes.name: Maximal admissible ball
nodes.statement: Further, $B$ will be called \emph{maximal admissible} if $r_B = \min(1,1/\mod{c_B})$.

nodes.name: Gaussian (1,r)-atom
nodes.statement: Now let $r\in(1,\infty]$. A \emph{Gaussian} $(1,r)$-\emph{atom} is either the constant function $1$ or a function $a$ in $L^r(\gamma)$ supported in an admissible ball $B$ and such that \begin{equation} \int a \, \,\mathrm{d} \gamma =0 \qquad \textnormal{and}\qquad \norm{a}{r}\leq \gamma(B)^{1/r-1};\ \end{equation} here and in the whole paper, $\norm{\cdot}{r}$ denotes the norm in $L^r(\gamma)$.
differentia: either the constant function $1$ or a function $a$ in $L^r(\gamma)$ supported in an admissible ball $B$
nodes.statement_short: A Gaussian (1,r)-atom is the constant 1 or a mean-zero L^r function on an admissible ball B with ||a||_r <= gamma(B)^{1/r-1}.

nodes.name: Atom associated to a ball
nodes.statement: In the latter case, we say that the atom $a$ is associated to the ball $B $.

nodes.name: Atomic Hardy space H^{1,r}(gamma)
nodes.statement: The space $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ is then the vector space of all functions $f$ in $\lu{\gamma}$ that admit a decomposition of the form $\sum_j \lambda_j \, a_j$ where the $a_j$ are Gaussian $(1,r)$-atoms and the sequence of complex numbers $\{\lambda_j\}$ is summable.
nodes.genus: vector space of all functions $f$ in $\lu{\gamma}$
differentia: admit a decomposition of the form $\sum_j \lambda_j \, a_j$ where the $a_j$ are Gaussian $(1,r)$-atoms and the sequence of complex numbers $\{\lambda_j\}$ is summable

nodes.name: Norm of H^{1,r}(gamma)
nodes.statement: The norm of $f$ in $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ is defined as the infimum of $\sum_j\mod{\lambda_j}$ over all representations of $f$ as above.

nodes.name: Coincidence of H^{1,r}(gamma) for 1<r<infinity
nodes.statement: In \cite{MM} the spaces $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ were defined and proved to coincide for all $1<r<\infty$, with equivalent norms.
conclusions: the spaces $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ were defined and proved to coincide for all $1<r<\infty$, with equivalent norms

nodes.name: Hardy space H^1(gamma)
nodes.statement: Once this is established, we shall denote the space by $H^1(\gamma)$ and use the $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ norm.

nodes.name: Atom (shorthand)
nodes.statement: Further, we shall frequently write atom for $(1,\infty)$-atom.

nodes.name: BMO(gamma)
nodes.statement: The space $BMO(\gamma)$ consists of all functions $f$ in $L^1 (\gamma)$ such that $$ \sup_{B\in\mathcal{B}_1} \frac{1}{\gamma(B)}\int_B\mod{f-f_B}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma< \infty, $$ where $f_B$ denotes the mean value of $f$ on $B$, taken with respect to the Gauss measure.
nodes.statement_short: BMO(gamma): L^1(gamma) functions with bounded mean oscillation over admissible balls.

nodes.name: Norm of BMO(gamma)
nodes.statement: The norm of a function in $BMO(\gamma)$ is $$ \norm{f}{BMO(\gamma)}=\norm{f}{1}+\sup_{B\in\mathcal{B}_1} \frac{1} {\gamma(B)}\int_B\mod{f-f_B}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma. $$

nodes.name: Scale independence of H^1(gamma) and BMO(gamma)
nodes.statement: If, in the definitions of $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$, we replace the family $\mathcal{B}_1$ of admissible balls at scale $1$ by $\mathcal{B}_s$ for any fixed $s>0$, we obtain the same spaces with equivalent norms, see \cite{MM}.
assumptions: in the definitions of $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$, we replace the family $\mathcal{B}_1$ of admissible balls at scale $1$ by $\mathcal{B}_s$ for any fixed $s>0$
conclusions: we obtain the same spaces with equivalent norms

nodes.name: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator
nodes.statement: The main motivation for introducing these two spaces was to provide endpoint estimates for singular integrals associated to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator $\mathcal{L}=-(1/2)\Delta+x\cdot\nabla$, a natural self-adjoint Laplacian on $L^2(\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Endpoint bounds for imaginary powers and Riesz transforms of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator
nodes.statement: Indeed, in \cite{MM} the first two authors proved that the imaginary powers of $\mathcal{L}$ are bounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$ and from $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$ and that Riesz transforms of the form $\nabla^ \alpha\mathcal{L}^{-\mod{\alpha}}$ and of any order are bounded from $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$.
conclusions: the imaginary powers of $\mathcal{L}$ are bounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$ and from  $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$
Riesz transforms of the form $\nabla^ \alpha\mathcal{L}^{-\mod{\alpha}}$ and of any order are bounded from $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$

nodes.name: First-order Riesz transforms: endpoint bounds in dimension one
nodes.statement: In a recent paper \cite{MMS2}, the authors proved that boundedness from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$ and from $L^\infty(\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$ holds for any first-order Riesz transform in dimension one, but not always in higher dimension.
conclusions: boundedness from  $\huat{\gamma}$ to  $L^1(\gamma)$ and  from  $L^\infty(\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$ holds  for any first-order Riesz transform in   dimension one, but not always in higher dimension

nodes.name: Duality, John-Nirenberg inequality and interpolation for H^1(gamma)
nodes.statement: In particular, the topological dual of $\huat{\gamma}$ is isomorphic to $BMO(\gamma)$, an inequality of John-Nirenberg type holds for functions in $BMO(\gamma)$ and the spaces $L^p(\gamma)$ are intermediate spaces between $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$ for the real and the complex interpolation methods.
conclusions: the topological dual of $\huat{\gamma}$ is isomorphic to $BMO(\gamma)$
an inequality of John-Nirenberg type holds for functions in $BMO(\gamma)$
the spaces $L^p(\gamma)$ are intermediate spaces between $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$ for the real and the complex interpolation methods

nodes.name: Unboundedness of first-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Riesz transforms in higher dimension
nodes.statement: As shown in \cite{MMS2}, in higher dimension the first-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Riesz transforms $\partial_j\mathcal{L}^{-1/2}$ are unbounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$; here $\partial_j = \partial/\partial_{x_j}$.
conclusions: the first-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Riesz transforms $\partial_j\mathcal{L}^{-1/2}$ are unbounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Grand maximal function characterisation of H^1(lambda)
nodes.statement: We recall that the classical space $H^1(\lambda)$ can be characterised as the space of all functions $f$ in $L^1(\lambda)$ whose \emph{grand maximal function} \begin{equation} \mathcal{M} f(x)=\sup\set{\mod{\phi_t*f(x)}: {\phi\in \Phi},\, t>0} \end{equation} is also in $L^1(\lambda)$.
conclusions: the classical space $H^1(\lambda)$ can be characterised as the space of all functions $f$ in $L^1(\lambda)$ whose \emph{grand maximal function}
is also in $L^1(\lambda)$
nodes.statement_short: Classical H^1(lambda) consists of the L^1 functions whose grand maximal function M f is integrable.

nodes.name: Test function class Phi and dilations phi_t
nodes.statement: Here $\Phi=\set{\phi \in C_c^1\big(B(0,1)\big): \mod{D^{\alpha}\phi}\le 1 \: \mathrm{for} \: \mod{\alpha}=0,1}$ and $\phi_t(x)=t^{-n}\phi(x/t)$.

nodes.name: Local grand maximal function
nodes.statement: To characterise $H^1(\gamma)$, we introduce the \emph{local grand maximal function} defined on $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^n,\gamma)$ by $$ \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f(x)=\sup\set{\mod{\phi_t*f(x)}: {\phi\in \Phi},\: 0<t< \min(1, 1/|x|)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: M_loc f(x): sup of |phi_t * f(x)| over phi in Phi and admissible scales 0<t<min(1,1/|x|).

nodes.name: Global condition E(f)
nodes.statement: Moreover, \emph {in dimension one} $\huat{\gamma}$ can be characterised as the space of all functions $f$ in $L^1(\gamma)$ satisfying $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \in L^1(\gamma)$ and the following additional \emph{global} condition \begin{equation} E(f)=\int_{0}^\infty x\ \left(\mod{\int_x^\infty f\,\mathrm{d}\gamma}+\mod{\int_{- \infty}^{-x} f\,\mathrm{d} \gamma}\right) \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)<\infty. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Announces the 1-D characterisation and defines the global condition E(f): weighted integral of tail masses of f is finite.

nodes.name: Electrical charge interpretation of the global condition
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, if we interpret a function $f$ as a density of electrical charge on the real line, this global condition says that the positive and negative charges nearly balance out, so that the net charges inside the intervals $(-\infty,-x)$ and $(x,\infty)$ decay sufficiently fast as $x$ approaches $+\infty$. The condition is violated when the distance between the positive and the negative charges increases too much or the charges do not decay sufficiently fast at infinity.
nodes.statement_short: E(f)<infinity says positive and negative charges of f nearly balance so tail net charges decay fast.

nodes.name: Function with M_loc f in L^1 but E(f) infinite
nodes.statement: For instance, let $(a_n)_1^\infty$ and $(a_n')_1^\infty$ be increasing sequences in $(2, \infty)$ such that \[ a_n + 2/a_n < a_n' \quad \mathrm{and} \quad a_n' + 2/a_n' < a_{n+1} < 2a_n \] for all $n$. Then set \begin{equation} f = \sum_1^\infty c_n \left(\frac{\chi_{(a_n,a_n+1/a_n)}}{\gamma(a_n,a_n+1/a_n)} -\frac{\chi_{(a_n',a_n'+1/a_n')}}{\gamma(a_n',a_n'+1/a_n')}\right) \end{equation} for some $c_n > 0$. One easily verifies that $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \in L^1(\gamma)$ if and only if $\sum c_n < \infty$. But the global condition $E(f) < \infty$ is equivalent to $\sum c_n a_n(a_n' - a_n) < \infty$, which is here a stronger condition.
nodes.statement_short: Sums of normalised indicator dipoles: M_loc f in L^1 iff sum c_n finite, but E(f) finite needs the stronger sum c_n a_n(a_n'-a_n) finite.

nodes.name: Maximal characterisation of H^1(gamma) in higher dimension
nodes.statement: We have not been able to find a similar characterisation of $\huat {\gamma}$ in higher dimension.

nodes.name: Equivalence of E(f) and E_+(f) for nonnegative f in dimension one
nodes.statement: Observe that for $n=1$ and $f \ge 0$, Fubini's theorem implies that the conditions $E(f)<\infty$ and $E_+(f)<\infty$ are equivalent.
conclusions: the conditions $E(f)<\infty$ and $E_+(f)<\infty$ are equivalent

nodes.name: Equivalence of Gauss and Lebesgue measures on admissible balls
nodes.statement: In the following we use repeatedly the fact that on admissible balls at a fixed scale $s$, the Gauss and the Lebesgue measures are equivalent, i.e., there exists a constant $C(s)$ such that for every measurable subset $E$ of $B\in\mathcal{B}_s$ \begin{equation} C(s)^{-1} \gamma(E)\le \,\gamma_0(c_B) \lambda(E)\le\,C(s)\gamma (E). \end{equation}
assumptions: admissible balls at a fixed scale $s$
conclusions: the Gauss and the Lebesgue measures are equivalent
nodes.statement_short: On balls admissible at scale s, gamma(E) and gamma_0(c_B) lambda(E) are comparable with constant C(s).

nodes.name: Gauss measure is doubling on admissible balls
nodes.statement: In particular this implies that the Gauss measure is doubling on balls in $\mathcal{B}_s$, with a constant that depends on $s$ (see \cite [{Prop. 2.1}]{MM}).
conclusions: the Gauss measure is doubling on balls in $\mathcal{B}_s$, with a  constant that depends on $s$

nodes.name: Sub-balls of admissible balls are admissible
nodes.statement: Further, it is straightforward to see that if $B'\subset B$ are two balls and $B\in \mathcal{B}_s$ then $B'$ is also in $\mathcal{B}_s$.
conclusions: $B'$ is also in $\mathcal{B}_s$

nodes.name: Dilated ball rho B
nodes.statement: Given a ball $B$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and a positive number $\rho$, we shall denote by $\rho B$ the ball with the same centre and with radius $\rho r_B$.

nodes.name: Constant convention C
nodes.statement: In the following $C$ denotes a constant whose value may change from occurrence to occurrence and which depends only on the dimension $n$, except when otherwise explicitly stated.

nodes.name: Lebesgue atoms
nodes.statement: It deals with the classical Hardy space $H^1(\lambda)$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure and the associated standard $(1,\infty)$-atoms, called Lebesgue atoms below.

nodes.name: Atomic decomposition of compactly supported H^1(lambda) functions
nodes.statement: If $g\in H^1(\lambda)$ and the support of $g$ is contained in a ball $B$, then $g$ has an atomic decomposition $g=\sum_k\lambda_k a_k$ where the $a_k$ are Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atoms associated to balls contained in $2B$ and \begin{equation} \sum_k \mod{\lambda_k}\le C\,\norm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. \end{equation}
assumptions: the support of $g$ is contained in a ball $B$
conclusions: $g$ has an atomic decomposition $g=\sum_k\lambda_k a_k$ where the $a_k$ are Lebesgue  $(1,\infty)$-atoms associated to balls contained in $2B$
nodes.statement_short: An H^1(lambda) function supported in a ball B decomposes into Lebesgue atoms on balls inside 2B with controlled coefficients.
nodes.label: cptsupp

nodes.name: Coincidence of H^{1,r}(gamma) and H^{1,infinity}(gamma)
nodes.statement: For every $r$ in $(1,\infty)$, the spaces $H^{1,r} (\gamma)$ and $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ coincide, with equivalent norms.
conclusions: the spaces  $H^{1,r} (\gamma)$ and $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ coincide, with equivalent norms
also_stated_at: In Section \ref{s:prel} we complement this by proving that they coincide also with the space $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$.
nodes.label: 1infty

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement_short: Multiply a Gaussian (1,r)-atom by gamma_0 to get a Lebesgue atom, decompose it via Lemma 2.1, and divide back by gamma_0.

nodes.name: Support of the local grand maximal function
nodes.statement: If $f \in L^1(\gamma)$ is supported in the admissible ball $B$, then $\mathrm{supp}\, \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f$ is contained in the ball $B' = B(c_B, R)$, where $R = 4 \min(1, 1/|c_B|).$
assumptions: $f \in L^1(\gamma)$ is supported in the admissible ball $B$
conclusions: $\mathrm{supp}\, \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f$ is contained in the ball   $B' = B(c_B, R)$, where $R = 4 \min(1, 1/|c_B|).$
nodes.label: supp

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathrm{supp}\, \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f$. We write $\rho = |x|$ and $c = |c_B|,$ so that $B \subset B(c_B, \min(1,1/c))$. The balls $B$ and $B(x, \min(1,1/\rho))$ must intersect, and so \begin{equation} |x-c_B| \le \min(1,1/c) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation} To prove the lemma, it is enough to show that \begin{equation} \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3 \min(1,1/c), \end{equation} since it then follows that $x \in B'$. Now $c - \rho \le |x-c_B|$, so that (\ref{eq:dist}) implies \[ c - \min(1,1/c) \le \rho + \min(1,1/\rho). \] Considering the cases $c \le 1$ and $c > 1$, we conclude from this that \begin{equation} \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation} The function $t \mapsto t^{-1} - t, \;\; t>0$, and its inverse are clearly decreasing. Considering the values of this function at $t = \min(1,1/c)$ and $\min(1,1/\rho)/3$, we see that (\ref{eq:3}) is equivalent to \[ \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho). \] Because of (\ref{eq:le}), this inequality follows if \[ \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho) \] or equivalently $\frac43 \min(1,1/\rho) \le 2\max(1,\rho),$ which is trivially true. We have proved (\ref{eq:3}) and the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Elementary inequalities between min(1,1/|x|) and min(1,1/|c_B|) using monotonicity of t^{-1}-t.

nodes.name: H^1(gamma) implies M_loc f in L^1(gamma)
nodes.statement: If $f$ is in $\huat{\gamma}$, then $ \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and \[ \norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f}{1}\le C\norm{ f}{H^1(\gamma)}. \]
conclusions: $ \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$
\norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f}{1}\le C\norm{ f}{H^1(\gamma)}
also_stated_at: In Section \ref{maxchar1} we shall prove that, in arbitrary dimension, $f\in \huat{\gamma}$ implies $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$.
nodes.label: necn

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: We shall prove that for any Gaussian atom $a$ \begin{equation} \norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} a}{1}\le C, \end{equation} from which the lemma follows. \par Since (\ref{MaEa}) is obvious if $a$ is the constant function $1$, we assume that $a$ is associated to an admissible ball $B$. By the preceding lemma, $\mathrm{supp}\, \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f$ is contained in the ball denoted $B'$. \par The integral of $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} a$ over $2B$ with respect to $\gamma$ is no larger than $C$, since $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a \le C \sup |a| \le C/\gamma(B)$. To estimate $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a$ at a point $x$ in the remaining set $B'\setminus 2B$, we take $\phi \in \Phi$ and $0 < t < \min(1,1/\mod{x})$ and estimate $a*\phi_t(x)$. We can assume that $t > d(x, B)$ so that $t > |x-c_B|/2$, since otherwise $\phi_t*a(x)$ will vanish. Write \begin{equation} \phi_t*a(x) = t^{-n} \int \left(\phi\big(\frac{x-y}t\big) -\phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big)\right)\,a(y) \,\mathrm{d} y + t^{-n} \phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big) \int a(y) \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{equation} Here the first term to the right can be estimated in a standard way by $$ C t^{-n-1} \int_B |y-c_B| \, |a(y)| \,\mathrm{d} y \le C\ |x-c_B|^{-n-1}\ r_B\ \gamma_0(c_B)^{-1}. $$ To deal with the second term, we estimate $\int a(y)\,\mathrm{d} y$, knowing that the integral of $a$ against $\gamma$ vanishes. Thus $$ \int a(y)\,\mathrm{d} y = \int a(y) \frac{\gamma_0(c_B) - \gamma_0(y)}{\gamma_0(c_B)}\,\mathrm{d} y. $$ The fraction appearing here is \begin{equation} e^{|c_B|^2}\left(e^{-|c_B|^2} - e^{-|y|^2}\right) = 1 - e^{(c_B-y)\cdot(c_B+y)}, \end{equation} and the last exponent stays bounded for $y \in B$. nodes.name: Claim: decay of M g off 2B
nodes.statement:
We claim that the grand maximal function of $g$ satisfies  egin{equation} \mathcal{M} g(x)\le\, rac{C\,
orm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}\qquad orall x
otin 2B. \end{equation} To prove this, take $x 
otin 2B$ and observe that $$ \mathcal{M} g(x) =\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\, \sup_{t\ge d(x,B)}\mod{\phi_t*g(x)}, $$ since $\phi_t*g(x)=0$ for $0<t < d(x,B)$. Because of the vanishing integral of $g$, one has for $\phi\in \Phi$ and $t \ge d(x,B)$  egin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*g(x)}&\le \,\int_{B}\mod{\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_B)}\,\mod{g (y)} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y) \ & \le\,C\,t^{-n-1}\int_{B}\mod{y-c_{B}}\,\mod{g(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y)\ &\le\,  rac{C\,r_{B}}{d(x,B)^{n+1}}\, 
orm{g}{1}\ &\le\,  rac{C }{\mod{B}}\, 
orm{g}{1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Claim M g <= C||g||_1/|B| outside 2B.

nodes.name: Reduce to large scales
nodes.statement: To prove this, take $x \notin 2B$ and observe that $$ \mathcal{M} g(x) =\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\, \sup_{t\ge d(x,B)}\mod{\phi_t*g(x)}, $$ since $\phi_t*g(x)=0$ for $0<t < d(x,B)$.
nodes.statement_short: Only scales t >= d(x,B) contribute.

nodes.name: Cancellation estimate
nodes.statement: Because of the vanishing integral of $g$, one has for $\phi\in \Phi$ and $t \ge d(x,B)$ \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*g(x)}&\le \,\int_{B}\mod{\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_B)}\,\mod{g (y)} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y) \\ & \le\,C\,t^{-n-1}\int_{B}\mod{y-c_{B}}\,\mod{g(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y)\\ &\le\, \frac{C\,r_{B}}{d(x,B)^{n+1}}\, \norm{g}{1}\\ &\le\, \frac{C }{\mod{B}}\, \norm{g}{1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use vanishing integral of g to bound phi_t*g(x).

nodes.name: Level sets inside 2B
nodes.statement: For each integer $k$, denote by $\Omega_k$ the level set $\set{x: \mathcal{M} g(x)>2^k}$. Then (\ref{MgIc}) implies that \begin{equation} \Omega_k\subset 2B \quad \textrm{when}\quad 2^k \ge \frac{C\, \norm{g}{1}\,}{ \mod{B}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Level sets Omega_k of M g lie in 2B for large k.

nodes.name: Whitney decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega_k=\bigcup_i Q^k_i$ be a Whitney decomposition of $ \Omega_k$ into closed cubes $Q^k_i, \; i \in \mathbb{N}$, whose interiors are disjoint, and whose diameters are comparable to $\delta$ times their distances from $\Omega_k^c$, where $\delta$ is a (small) positive constant to be chosen later. Define $\tilde{Q}_i^k$ as the cube with the same centre as $Q_i^k$ and side length expanded by a factor $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Whitney cubes of Omega_k and their doubles.

nodes.name: Bounded overlap
nodes.statement: Then $\bigcup_i\tilde{Q}^k_i= \Omega_k$ and the family $\set{\tilde{Q}^k_i: i\in \mathbb{N}}$ will have the bounded overlap property, uniformly in $k$, provided that $\delta$ is small enough.
nodes.statement_short: Doubled cubes cover Omega_k with bounded overlap.

nodes.name: Stein's atomic decomposition
nodes.statement: Proceeding as in the proof of the atomic decomposition for $H^1(\lambda)$ in \cite[p. 107--109]{St2}, one shows that there exists a decomposition \begin{equation} g=\sum_{k,i} A^k_i, \end{equation} with the following properties. \begin{itemize} \item[\hbox{\rm (i)}] Each function $A^k_i$ is supported in a ball $B^k_i$ that contains the cube $\tilde{Q}^k_i$ as well as those $\tilde{Q}^{k+1}_m$ that intersect $\tilde{Q}^k_i$. Moreover, if $\delta$ is sufficiently small, the ball $B^k_i$ is contained in $\Omega_k$ and for each $k$ the family $\set{B^k_i}_i$ has the bounded overlap property. \item[] \item[\hbox{\rm (ii)}] $A^k_i=\lambda_{k,i} \,a^k_i$, where $a^k_i$ is a Lebesgue atom associated to the ball $B^k_i$ and $$\sum_{k,i} \mod{\lambda_{k,i}}\le C\, \norm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. $$ \item[] \item[\hbox{\rm (iii)}] $\mod{A^k_i}\le C\,2^k$ for each $k$ and $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Follow Stein's construction to get a decomposition g = sum A_i^k with properties (i)-(iii).

nodes.name: Property (i)
nodes.statement: [\hbox{\rm (i)}] Each function $A^k_i$ is supported in a ball $B^k_i$ that contains the cube $\tilde{Q}^k_i$ as well as those $\tilde{Q}^{k+1}_m$ that intersect $\tilde{Q}^k_i$. Moreover, if $\delta$ is sufficiently small, the ball $B^k_i$ is contained in $\Omega_k$ and for each $k$ the family $\set{B^k_i}_i$ has the bounded overlap property.
nodes.statement_short: Supports in balls B_i^k inside Omega_k with bounded overlap.

nodes.name: Property (ii)
nodes.statement: [\hbox{\rm (ii)}] $A^k_i=\lambda_{k,i} \,a^k_i$, where $a^k_i$ is a Lebesgue atom associated to the ball $B^k_i$ and $$\sum_{k,i} \mod{\lambda_{k,i}}\le C\, \norm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: A_i^k are multiples of atoms with summable coefficients.

nodes.name: Property (iii)
nodes.statement: [\hbox{\rm (iii)}] $\mod{A^k_i}\le C\,2^k$ for each $k$ and $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise bound |A_i^k| <= C 2^k.

nodes.name: Split the sum
nodes.statement: We split the sum in (\ref{ad}) in two parts \begin{align*} g&=\sum_{B^k_i\not\subset 2B}A^k_i\ +\sum_{B^k_i\subset 2B} A^k_i =\Sigma_1+\Sigma_2. \end{align*} Clearly, $\Sigma_2$ is an atomic decomposition with atoms associated to balls contained in $2B$.
nodes.statement_short: Split into terms on balls not inside 2B and inside 2B.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Thus, it suffices to show that $ \Sigma_1$ is a multiple of an atom associated to $2B$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: Sigma_1 is a multiple of an atom on 2B.

nodes.name: Support and cancellation of Sigma_1
nodes.statement: And indeed, $\Sigma_1$ is supported in $2B $ and has integral zero, because it is the difference of $g$ and $ \Sigma_2$, both of which have these two properties.
nodes.statement_short: Sigma_1 is supported in 2B with integral zero.

nodes.name: Bound per level
nodes.statement: Moreover, by \hbox{\rm (i)}\ and \hbox{\rm (iii)}\ $$ \mod{\sum_i A^k_i}\le C\,2^k. $$
nodes.statement_short: Sum over i at level k is bounded by C 2^k.

nodes.name: Bound on Sigma_1
nodes.statement:
Hence by (ef{hi}) $$ \mod{\Sigma_1}\le\sum_{ 2^k \,<\,C\,
orm{g}{1}/\mod{B}}\mod {\sum_i A^k_i}\le  rac{C\,
orm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}\le  rac{C}{\mod {2B}}\,
orm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Sum geometric bounds over the levels below the threshold.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus $\Sigma_1$ is a multiple of an atom associated to $2B$. We thus have the desired atomic decomposition of $g$, and the norm estimate (\ref{ne}) also follows.
nodes.statement_short: Sigma_1 is a multiple of an atom; decomposition and norm bound follow.

nodes.name: Constants
nodes.statement: In this proof, the constants $C$ may depend on $r$ and $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Constants may depend on r and n.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: Since any Gaussian $(1,\infty)$-atom is also a Gaussian $(1,r)$-atom, $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ is a subspace of $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ and $\norm{f}{H^{1,r}(\gamma)}\le\norm{f}{H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)}$.
nodes.statement_short: (1,infinity)-atoms are (1,r)-atoms, giving one inclusion.

nodes.name: Take a (1,r)-atom
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that $a$ is a Gaussian $(1,r)$-atom associated to the ball $B \in \mathcal{B}_1$. Then the function $a\,\gamma_0$ is a multiple of a Lebesgue $(1,r)$-atom.
nodes.statement_short: For a Gaussian (1,r)-atom a, a gamma_0 is a multiple of a Lebesgue atom.

nodes.name: Verify Lebesgue atom
nodes.statement: Indeed, $\int a\gamma_0\,\mathrm{d}\lambda=\int a\,\mathrm{d}\gamma=0$ and, by the equivalence of the Gauss and Lebesgue measures on admissible balls, $$ \norm{a\gamma_0}{L^r(\lambda)}\le C\,\lambda(B)^{1/r-1}. $$ Hence, $a_0\gamma$ is in $H^1(\lambda)$ with norm at most $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Cancellation and L^r bound via measure equivalence.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{cptsupp}, it has a decomposition $$ a\,\gamma_0=\sum_j\lambda_j \alpha_j, $$ where each $\alpha_j$ is a Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atom associated to a ball $B_j$ contained in $2B$. Moreover $$ \sum_j\mod{\lambda_j}\le C, $$ and each $B_j$ is admissible at scale $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose a gamma_0 into Lebesgue atoms on balls in 2B.

nodes.name: Divide back by gamma_0
nodes.statement: Define $a_j=\alpha_j\,\gamma_0^{-1}$. Then $\int a_j\,\mathrm{d}\gamma=0$, and by the equivalence of the Gauss and Lebesgue measures on $B_j$ \begin{align*} \norm{a_j}{\infty}\le C \gamma(B_j)^{-1}. \end{align*} Thus the $a_j$ are multiples of Gaussian $(1,\infty)$-atoms.
nodes.statement_short: a_j = alpha_j/gamma_0 are multiples of Gaussian atoms.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $a=\sum_j\lambda_j a_j$, we conclude that $a \in H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ and \begin{equation} \norm{a}{H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)}\le\,C \sum_j\mod{\lambda_j}\le C. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: a lies in H^{1,infinity} with bounded norm.

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathrm{supp}\, \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f$. We write $\rho = |x|$ and $c = |c_B|,$ so that $B \subset B(c_B, \min(1,1/c))$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix x in the support; set rho=|x|, c=|c_B|.

nodes.name: Balls intersect
nodes.statement: The balls $B$ and $B(x, \min(1,1/\rho))$ must intersect, and so \begin{equation} |x-c_B| \le \min(1,1/c) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Intersection gives a distance bound.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: To prove the lemma, it is enough to show that \begin{equation} \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3 \min(1,1/c), \end{equation} since it then follows that $x \in B'$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show min(1,1/rho) <= 3 min(1,1/c).

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Now $c - \rho \le |x-c_B|$, so that (\ref{eq:dist}) implies \[ c - \min(1,1/c) \le \rho + \min(1,1/\rho). \]
nodes.statement_short: Derive c - min(1,1/c) <= rho + min(1,1/rho).

nodes.name: Cases c<=1, c>1
nodes.statement: Considering the cases $c \le 1$ and $c > 1$, we conclude from this that \begin{equation} \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation} The function $t \mapsto t^{-1} - t, \;\; t>0$, and its inverse are clearly decreasing.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis yields inequality (3.3); note monotonicity of t^{-1}-t.

nodes.name: Reformulate (3.2)
nodes.statement: Considering the values of this function at $t = \min(1,1/c)$ and $\min(1,1/\rho)/3$, we see that (\ref{eq:3}) is equivalent to \[ \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho). \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite (3.2) via the decreasing function.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Because of (\ref{eq:le}), this inequality follows if \[ \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho) \] or equivalently $\frac43 \min(1,1/\rho) \le 2\max(1,\rho),$ which is trivially true. We have proved (\ref{eq:3}) and the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a trivial inequality; lemma proved.

nodes.name: Reduce to atoms
nodes.statement: We shall prove that for any Gaussian atom $a$ \begin{equation} \norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} a}{1}\le C, \end{equation} from which the lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to bound ||M_loc a||_1 for atoms a.

nodes.name: Non-constant atom
nodes.statement: Since (\ref{MaEa}) is obvious if $a$ is the constant function $1$, we assume that $a$ is associated to an admissible ball $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Constant atom is trivial; take a on admissible ball B.

nodes.name: Support via Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: By the preceding lemma, $\mathrm{supp}\, \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f$ is contained in the ball denoted $B'$.
nodes.statement_short: Support of M_loc lies in B'.

nodes.name: Estimate on 2B
nodes.statement: The integral of $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} a$ over $2B$ with respect to $\gamma$ is no larger than $C$, since $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a \le C \sup |a| \le C/\gamma(B)$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial sup bound on 2B.

nodes.name: Setup on B'\2B
nodes.statement: To estimate $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a$ at a point $x$ in the remaining set $B'\setminus 2B$, we take $\phi \in \Phi$ and $0 < t < \min(1,1/\mod{x})$ and estimate $a*\phi_t(x)$. We can assume that $t > d(x, B)$ so that $t > |x-c_B|/2$, since otherwise $\phi_t*a(x)$ will vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Fix phi, t and restrict to t > d(x,B).

nodes.name: Split convolution
nodes.statement: Write \begin{equation} \phi_t*a(x) = t^{-n} \int \left(\phi\big(\frac{x-y}t\big) -\phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big)\right)\,a(y) \,\mathrm{d} y + t^{-n} \phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big) \int a(y) \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Split phi_t*a(x) into a difference term and a mean term.

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement: Here the first term to the right can be estimated in a standard way by $$ C t^{-n-1} \int_B |y-c_B| \, |a(y)| \,\mathrm{d} y \le C\ |x-c_B|^{-n-1}\ r_B\ \gamma_0(c_B)^{-1}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Standard estimate of the difference term.

nodes.name: Rewrite Lebesgue integral of a
nodes.statement: To deal with the second term, we estimate $\int a(y)\,\mathrm{d} y$, knowing that the integral of $a$ against $\gamma$ vanishes. Thus $$ \int a(y)\,\mathrm{d} y = \int a(y) \frac{\gamma_0(c_B) - \gamma_0(y)}{\gamma_0(c_B)}\,\mathrm{d} y. $$
nodes.statement_short: Use vanishing gamma-integral to rewrite int a dy.

nodes.name: Bound the fraction
nodes.statement: The fraction appearing here is \begin{equation} e^{|c_B|^2}\left(e^{-|c_B|^2} - e^{-|y|^2}\right) = 1 - e^{(c_B-y)\cdot(c_B+y)}, \end{equation} and the last exponent stays bounded for $y \in B$. Thus the modulus of the right-hand side of (\ref{eq:fraction}) is at most $C|c_B-y| |c_B+y| \le C r_B (1+|c_B|).$ Since $\int |a|\,d\gamma \le 1$, this implies \[ |\int a(y)\,\mathrm{d} y| \le C r_B (1+|c_B|) \gamma_0(c_B)^{-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The fraction is O(r_B(1+|c_B|)), bounding int a dy.

nodes.name: Second term
nodes.statement: For the last term in (\ref{eq:max}), we thus get the bound $C |x-c_B|^{-n} r_B (1+|c_B|) \gamma_0(c_B)^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound on the mean term.

nodes.name: Pointwise bound
nodes.statement: Putting things together, we conclude that for $x \in B'\setminus 2B$ $$ \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a(x) \le C |x-c_B|^{-n-1} r_B \gamma_0(c_B)^{-1} + C |x-c_B|^{-n} r_B (1+|c_B|) \gamma_0(c_B)^{-1}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Combined pointwise bound on B' minus 2B.

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement: An integration with respect to $\,\mathrm{d} \gamma$, or equivalently $\gamma_0 \,\mathrm{d} \lambda$, then leads to $$ \int_{B'\setminus 2B} \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a(x)\,\mathrm{d} \gamma(x) \le C + C r_B (1+|c_B|) \log\frac{\min(1,1/|c_B|)}{r_B} \le C, $$ and (\ref{MaEa}) is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate against gamma to get (3.4).

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f\in\huat{\gamma}$. Then $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$ by Lemma \ref{necn}. To prove the necessity of the condition $E(f)<\infty$, it suffices to show that $E(a)<C$ for all Gaussian atoms $a$. This is obvious for the exceptional atom $1$. If $a$ is associated to a ball $B \in \mathcal{B}_1$, it follows from the inequality $$ \mod{\int_{-\infty}^{-x} a\,\mathrm{d}\gamma}+\mod{\int_{x}^{\infty} a\,\mathrm{d} \gamma}\le \ {\bf 1}_B(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Necessity: M_loc f in L^1 by Lemma 3.2 and E(a) bounded for atoms.

nodes.name: M_loc f integrable
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f\in\huat{\gamma}$. Then $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$ by Lemma \ref{necn}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3.2.

nodes.name: Reduce E(f) to atoms
nodes.statement: To prove the necessity of the condition $E(f)<\infty$, it suffices to show that $E(a)<C$ for all Gaussian atoms $a$. This is obvious for the exceptional atom $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices E(a)<C for atoms.

nodes.name: E(a) for non-constant atoms
nodes.statement: If $a$ is associated to a ball $B \in \mathcal{B}_1$, it follows from the inequality $$ \mod{\int_{-\infty}^{-x} a\,\mathrm{d}\gamma}+\mod{\int_{x}^{\infty} a\,\mathrm{d} \gamma}\le \ {\bf 1}_B(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Tail integrals of a are bounded by the indicator of B.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume that $f$ is a function in $L^1(\gamma)$ such that $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E(f)<\infty$. We shall prove that $f\in H^1(\gamma)$, by constructing a Gaussian atomic decomposition $f= \sum_j\lambda_j\,a_j$ such that $\sum_j \mod{\lambda_j}\le C \big (\norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f}{1}+E(f)\big)$.
nodes.statement_short: Aim: atomic decomposition with coefficients bounded by ||M_loc f||_1+E(f).

nodes.name: n-dimensional part
nodes.statement: Most of the following argument, up to the decomposition (\ref{aat}), works also in the $n$-dimensional setting. Since we shall need it in the next section, we carry out that part in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: First part done in R^n for reuse.

nodes.name: Mean zero WLOG
nodes.statement: By subtracting a multiple of the exceptional atom $1$, we may without loss of generality assume that \begin{equation} \int f\,\mathrm{d}\gamma=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Assume int f d gamma = 0.

nodes.name: Covering and partition of unity
nodes.statement: Let $\set{B_j}$ be a covering of $\mathbb{R}^n$ by maximal admissible balls. We can choose this covering in such way that the family $\set{\frac12 B_j}$ is disjoint and $\set{4 B_j}$ has bounded overlap \cite[Lemma 2.4]{GMST1}. Fix a smooth nonnegative partition of unity $\set{\eta_j}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\mathrm{supp}\, \eta_j \subset B_j$ and $\eta_j=1$ on $\tfrac{1}{2}B_j$ and verifying $ \mod{\nabla\eta_j}\le C/r_{B_j}$. Thus $f=\sum_j f \eta_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Cover by maximal admissible balls with partition of unity eta_j.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.4 block
nodes.statement_short: Inner Lemma 3.4 and its proof.

nodes.name: Define b_j
nodes.statement: Continuing the proof of Theorem \ref{char}, we define $b_j\in\mathbb{C}$ for each $j \in \mathbb{N}$ by \begin{equation} \int_{-\infty}^\infty (f-b_j)\eta_j \,\mathrm{d} \gamma =0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose constants b_j making (f-b_j)eta_j mean zero.

nodes.name: Bound on b_j
nodes.statement: Note that since $\eta_j=1$ on $\frac12 B_j$, \begin{equation} \mod{b_j} = \left|\frac{\int{f\eta_j}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma} {\int \eta_j \,\mathrm{d} \gamma}\right|\le C \frac{1}{\gamma(B_j)}{\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: b_j bounded by the average of |f| on B_j.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement: We now apply Lemma \ref{Lemma1} with $g=f - b_j$ and use the subadditivity of $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}}$ combined with (\ref{1st}), to get \begin{align} \int \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}}\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda&\le\,C\, \int_{4B_j} \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \, \gamma_0(c_{B_j})\,\mathrm{d}\lambda \,+\,C\, \frac {\gamma(4B_j)}{\gamma(B_j)}\int_{B_j} \mod{f}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma \nonumber \\ &\le\,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d}\gamma. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound M_loc of the local pieces by M_loc f on 4B_j.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.5 block
nodes.statement: \begin{lemma} The function $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ is in $H^1(\lambda)$ and \begin{equation} \norm{(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0}{H^1(\lambda)}\le\,\, \int_{4B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d} \gamma. \end{equation} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} By the maximal characterisation of the classical space $H^1(\lambda) $, it suffices to show that \begin{equation} \int\mathcal{M}\left( (f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\right)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)\le \,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d}\gamma. \end{equation} Because of (\ref{3d}), all that needs to be verified is that \begin{equation} \int\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\ \sup_{t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})} \mod{((f-b_j) \eta_j\gamma_0\big)*\phi_t(x)}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x) \le \,C\, \int_{4B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d} \gamma. \end{equation} To prove (\ref{6th}), we split the integral in the left-hand side into the sum $$ \int_{4B_j}\cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)+\int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x). $$ If $x\in 4B_j$, then for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})$ \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le t^{-n} \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)-b_j}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma(y)\\ &\le (1+\mod{x})^n\int _{B_j}\big(\mod{f(y)}+\mod{b_j}\big)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma (y) \\ \qquad&\le C\,(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n\ \,\int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(y), \end{align*} the last inequality because of (\ref{1st}). Hence \begin{align*} \int_{4B_j} \cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)\, \le \,C\, \ \mod {4B_j}\ (1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n \int_{B_j}\mod{f}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma \, \le\, C\,\int_{B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d}\gamma . \end{align*} If $x\in (4B_j)^c$, we take $\phi$ and $t$ as before and observe that we can assume that $t> d(x, B_j)$, since otherwise the convolution in (\ref{6th}) will vanish. In view of (\ref{mz}) and (\ref{1st}), we then get \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le\int _{B_j}\mod {\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_{B_j})}\ \mod{ f(y)-b_j}\,\eta_j(y) \,\mathrm{d} \gamma(y) \\ &\le\,C\, t^{-n-1} \int_{B_j} \mod{y-c_{B_j}}\,\mod{f(y)-b_j}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma (y)\\ &\le \,C\,\frac{1}{d(x,B_j)^{n+1}} r_{B_j}\, \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(y). \end{align*} This implies that $$ \int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)\le C\,\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\le C\, \int_{B_j} \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d} \gamma. $$ We have proved (\ref{6th}) and the lemma. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Inner Lemma 3.5 and its proof.

nodes.name: Atomic decomposition of local pieces
nodes.statement: We can now finish the proof of Theorem \ref{char}. By Lemmata \ref{Lemma2} and \ref{cptsupp}, each function $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ has an atomic decomposition $ \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \alpha_{jk}$ where the $\alpha_{jk}$ are Lebesgue atoms with supports in $2B_j$ and $$ \sum_k \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le \,C\, \int_{4B_j} \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d}\gamma. $$
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 3.5 and 2.1 give Lebesgue atoms on 2B_j.

nodes.name: Back to Gaussian atoms
nodes.statement: As we saw in the proof of Theorem \ref{1infty}, each $a_{jk}=\gamma_0^{-1} \alpha_{jk}$ is a multiple of a Gaussian atom, with a factor which is independent of $j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: As in Theorem 2.2, gamma_0^{-1} alpha_jk are multiples of Gaussian atoms.

nodes.name: Decomposition of f
nodes.statement: Thus \begin{align} f=\sum_j (f-b_j)\eta_j +\sum_j b_j \eta_j = \sum_j \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \,a_{jk} +\sum_j b_j \eta_j. \end{align} and $$ \sum_{j,k} \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le \sum_j \int_{4B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d}\gamma \le \,C\, \norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f}{L^1(\gamma)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: f = atomic part + sum b_j eta_j with controlled coefficients.

nodes.name: Remaining term
nodes.statement: To complete the proof of Theorem \ref{char}, we need to find an atomic decomposition of $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$. It is here that we must restrict ourselves to the one-dimensional case and that the global condition $E(f) <\infty$ plays a role.
nodes.statement_short: Remains to decompose sum b_j eta_j; here n=1 and E(f) are needed.

nodes.name: Intervals I_j
nodes.statement: Choose the intervals $I_0=(-1,1)$, $I_j=(\sqrt{j-1}, \sqrt{j+1})$ for $j\ge 1$ and $I_j=-I_{\mod{j}}$ for $j\le -1$. The intervals $I_j$ have essentially the same properties as the balls $B_j$ introduced above, and we can use them instead of the $B_j$ to construct $\eta_j$ and $b_j$ as before.
nodes.statement_short: Use intervals I_j in place of B_j.

nodes.name: Normalise and define mu_k
nodes.statement: To decompose now $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$, we first normalise the functions $\eta_j$, letting \[ \tilde{\eta}_j = \frac{\eta_j}{\int \eta_j \,\mathrm{d} \gamma}. \] Then $b_j\eta_j = \int f \eta_j \,\mathrm{d} \gamma \; \tilde{\eta}_j$, and clearly \[ \sum_{j\ge k}\int f \eta_j \,\mathrm{d} \gamma = \int f \mu_k \,\mathrm{d} \gamma, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}, \] where $\mu_k(x) = \sum_{j\ge k} \eta_j(x).$
nodes.statement_short: Normalise eta_j and introduce tail sums mu_k.

nodes.name: Summation by parts
nodes.statement: Notice that $\int f \mu_k \,\mathrm{d} \gamma \to 0$ as $k \to \pm \infty$, in view of (\ref{int0}). A summation by parts now yields \begin{equation} \sum_{j\in \mathbb{Z}} \int f \eta_j \,\mathrm{d} \gamma \; \tilde{\eta}_j = \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} \int f \mu_k \,\mathrm{d} \gamma \; (\tilde{\eta}_k - \tilde{\eta}_{k-1}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Summation by parts gives decomposition (3.16).

nodes.name: Reduce to coefficient estimate
nodes.statement: But $\tilde{\eta}_k - \tilde{\eta}_{k-1}$ is $C$ times a Gaussian atom, if we use admissible balls at some scale $s>1$ in the definition of atoms. Thus (\ref{eq:**}) is our desired atomic decomposition of $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$, provided we can estimate the coefficients by showing that \begin{equation} \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}}\left| \int f \mu_k \,\mathrm{d} \gamma \right| \le\,C\,\left(\norm{f}{1}+ E(f)\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Differences are atoms at a larger scale; suffices to prove (3.17).

nodes.name: Fubini
nodes.statement: To this end, observe that $$ \int f \mu_k \,\mathrm{d} \gamma =\int f(x)\int_{-\infty}^x\mu'_k(y)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x)=\int \mu'_k(y)\int_y^\infty f(x)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y). $$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite int f mu_k via Fubini.

nodes.name: Coefficient estimate
nodes.statement: Since the support of $\mu'_k$ is contained in $I_k$ and $$ \mod{\mu_k'(y)}\,\le\, \frac{C}{\mod{I_k}}\,\le\, C \,\big(1+\mod{c_{I_k}} \big), $$ we obtain, using also the bounded overlap of the $I_j$, \begin{align*} \sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}}\left| \int f \mu_k \,\mathrm{d} \gamma \right| &\,\le\,C \sum_k\int_{I_k}\big(1+\mod{c_{I_k}}\big)\ \mod{\int_y^\infty f(x)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x)}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y) \\ &\le C\int_{-\infty}^\infty (1+\mod{y}) \mod{\int_y^\infty f\,\mathrm{d} \gamma}\,\mathrm{d} \lambda(y) \\ &= C\int_{0}^\infty (1+y) \left(\mod{\int_y^\infty f\,\mathrm{d} \gamma}+\mod{\int_{-y} ^\infty f\,\mathrm{d} \gamma}\right)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(y) \\ &\le\, C\big(\norm{f}{1}+ \,E(f)\big); \end{align*} here we used (\ref{int0}). This concludes the proof of Theorem \ref{char}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the coefficients by ||f||_1 + E(f).

nodes.name: Support via Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Since the support of $\eta_j$ is contained in $B_j$, the support of $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} (g\eta_j\gamma_0)$ is contained in the ball $4B_j$, because of Lemma \ref{supp}.
nodes.statement_short: Support of M_loc(g eta_j gamma_0) lies in 4B_j.

nodes.name: Modified test function
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $x \in 4B_j$ $$ \phi_t*(g\eta_j\gamma_0)(x)=\gamma_0(c_{B_j})\ \tilde{\phi}_t*g(x), $$ where $\tilde{\phi}(z)=\phi(z)\eta_j(x-tz)\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_ {B_j})$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite convolution with tilde phi.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Thus, to prove (\ref{2maxf}) it suffices to show that there exists a constant $C$ such that $\tilde{\phi}\in C\Phi$ for $x\in 4B_j$ and $0<t < \min(1, 1/\mod{x})$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices tilde phi in C Phi.

nodes.name: Check tilde phi in C Phi
nodes.statement:
The support of $	ilde{\phi}$ is contained in $B(0,1)$ and $$ \mod{	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le  rac{\gamma_0(x-tz)}{\gamma_0(c_{B_j})}\le C, $$ because for $|z| \le 1$  egin{align*} \mod{x-tz-c_{B_j}}\le \mod{x-c_{B_j}}+\mod{tz} \le C\,{\min(1, 1/\mod{c_{B_j}})}. \end{align*} Similarly $\mod{
abla	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le C$, because the gradients $ 
abla_z\eta_j (x-tz)$ and $
abla_z\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_{B_j})$ give the factors $t(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})$ and $t\mod{x-tz}\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_{B_j})$, respectively, both of which are bounded. This concludes the proof of Lemma ef{Lemma1}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound tilde phi and its gradient.

nodes.name: Maximal characterisation
nodes.statement: By the maximal characterisation of the classical space $H^1(\lambda) $, it suffices to show that \begin{equation} \int\mathcal{M}\left( (f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\right)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)\le \,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d}\gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to bound the grand maximal function in L^1(lambda).

nodes.name: Large scales
nodes.statement: Because of (\ref{3d}), all that needs to be verified is that \begin{equation} \int\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\ \sup_{t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})} \mod{((f-b_j) \eta_j\gamma_0\big)*\phi_t(x)}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x) \le \,C\, \int_{4B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d} \gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Only large scales t >= min(1,1/|x|) remain.

nodes.name: Split the integral
nodes.statement: To prove (\ref{6th}), we split the integral in the left-hand side into the sum $$ \int_{4B_j}\cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)+\int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Split into 4B_j and its complement.

nodes.name: x in 4B_j
nodes.statement: If $x\in 4B_j$, then for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})$ \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le t^{-n} \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)-b_j}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma(y)\\ &\le (1+\mod{x})^n\int _{B_j}\big(\mod{f(y)}+\mod{b_j}\big)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma (y) \\ \qquad&\le C\,(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n\ \,\int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(y), \end{align*} the last inequality because of (\ref{1st}). Hence \begin{align*} \int_{4B_j} \cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)\, \le \,C\, \ \mod {4B_j}\ (1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n \int_{B_j}\mod{f}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma \, \le\, C\,\int_{B_j}\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d}\gamma . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Trivial bound on 4B_j.

nodes.name: x outside 4B_j
nodes.statement: If $x\in (4B_j)^c$, we take $\phi$ and $t$ as before and observe that we can assume that $t> d(x, B_j)$, since otherwise the convolution in (\ref{6th}) will vanish. In view of (\ref{mz}) and (\ref{1st}), we then get \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le\int _{B_j}\mod {\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_{B_j})}\ \mod{ f(y)-b_j}\,\eta_j(y) \,\mathrm{d} \gamma(y) \\ &\le\,C\, t^{-n-1} \int_{B_j} \mod{y-c_{B_j}}\,\mod{f(y)-b_j}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma (y)\\ &\le \,C\,\frac{1}{d(x,B_j)^{n+1}} r_{B_j}\, \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(y). \end{align*} This implies that $$ \int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \,\mathrm{d}\lambda(x)\le C\,\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\le C\, \int_{B_j} \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f \,\mathrm{d} \gamma. $$ We have proved (\ref{6th}) and the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Cancellation bound off 4B_j; integrate.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: We shall construct atoms whose supports form a chain connecting $B(0,1)$ to $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of atoms from B(0,1) to B.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Chain of balls
nodes.statement: First we define a finite sequence of maximal admissible balls \[ \tilde{B} _0 = B(0,1),\, \tilde{B}_1, \ldots, \tilde{B}_{N }, \] all with centres $c_{\tilde{B}_{j}}$ on the segment $[0, c_B]$. The absolute values $\rho_j= |c_{\tilde{B}_{j}}|$ shall be increasing in $j$, and the boundary $\partial \tilde{B}_j$ shall contain $c_{\tilde{B}_{j-1}}$ for $j = 1,\ldots,N-1$, which means that \begin{align} \rho_{j} - \frac{1}{\rho_{j}}=\rho_{j-1}, \qquad j=1, \ldots,N-1, \end{align} and $\rho_{0} = 0, \; \;\rho_{1} = 1$. Finally, $N$ is defined so that $\tilde{B}_{N-1}$ is the first ball of the sequence that contains $c_B$, and $\tilde{B}_{N } = B.$
nodes.statement_short: Define maximal admissible balls along [0,c_B].
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Count balls
nodes.statement: Squaring (\ref{recursive}), we get $$ \rho_{j}^2-\rho_{j-1}^2=2 - \frac1{\rho_{j}^2}\ge1, $$ so that $\rho_{N-1}^2 \ge N-1$. It follows that \begin{equation} N \le |c_B|^2 + 1. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Define phi_j and g_j
nodes.statement: Next, we denote by $B _j, \;\;j=1,\ldots, N$, the largest ball contained in $\tilde{B}_j \cap\tilde{B}_{j-1} $. Notice that the three balls $\tilde{B}_j, \tilde{B}_{j-1}$ and $B _j$ have comparable radii and comparable Gaussian measures. Define now functions $\phi _j$ and $g _j$ by setting \begin{align*} \phi _j&=\gamma(B _j )^{-1} {\mathbf{1}}_{B _j } \quad j=1,\ldots,N, \\ g _j &= \int g \,\mathrm{d}\gamma\, \left(\phi_{j} -\phi _{j-1} \right), \quad j=1,\ldots,N, \\ g_{N+1} &=g -\int g \,\mathrm{d} \gamma \: \phi_{N}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Normalised indicators phi_j and telescoping pieces g_j.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Telescoping sum
nodes.statement: Clearly, \begin{equation} g-\int g\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\: \phi_0 = \sum_{j=1}^{N+1} g _j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: g - (int g) phi_0 = sum g_j.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Each g_j atom-like
nodes.statement: Each function $g _j$ is a multiple of an atom. Indeed, its integral against $\gamma$ vanishes.
nodes.statement_short: Each g_j has integral zero.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Sup bounds
nodes.statement:
Moreover, if $1 \le j \le N$, the support of $g _j$ is contained in $	ilde{B} _{j-1}$ and  egin{align*} 
orm{g _j}{\infty}\le (\gamma(B_{j})^{-1} + \gamma(B_{j-1})^{-1}) \int \mod{g}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\, \le \,C\, \gamma(	ilde{B}_{j-1})^{-1}\ \gamma (B)\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} The support of $\phi_{N+1}$ is contained in $B$ and  egin{align*} 
orm{g_{N+1}}{\infty}\le 
orm{g}{\infty}+\gamma(B)^ {-1}\int \mod{g}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma \le\,C\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} Thus $$ 
orm{g _j}{H^1(\gamma)}\le C\,\gamma(B)\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,N+1. $$
nodes.statement_short: Sup bounds give H^1 norms C gamma(B)||g||_inf.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Sum
nodes.statement:
Summing the coefficients in the atomic decomposition (ef{sumgj}), we then obtain via (ef{balls})  egin{align*} 
orm{g-\int g\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\,\phi_0}{\huat{\gamma}} \,\le\, C\, (N+1) \,\gamma(B) 
orm{g}{L^\infty} \, \le\,C (1+\mod{c_B}^2)\,\gamma(B) \,
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} The proof of the lemma is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Sum N+1 terms using N <= |c_B|^2+1.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Split off the mean
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a function in $L^1(\gamma)$ such that $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E_+(f)<~\infty$. Write $f=c(f)+f_0$, where $c(f)=\int f\,\mathrm{d}\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Write f = c(f) + f_0.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Reduce to f_0
nodes.statement: Since $c(f)$ is a multiple of the exceptional atom, it suffices to find an atomic decomposition of $f_0$. Note that $f_0$ satisfies $$ \mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f_0 \in L^1(\gamma) \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \int\mod{x}^2\, \mod{f_0(x)}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x)<\infty. $$
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to decompose f_0, which satisfies the hypotheses.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Reuse covering
nodes.statement: Let $\set{B_j}$ be the covering of $\mathbb{R}^n$ by maximal admissible balls and $\set{\eta_j}$ the corresponding partition of unity introduced in the proof of Theorem \ref{char}. As there, we choose numbers $b_j\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $$ \int_{-\infty}^\infty (f_0-b_j)\eta_j \,\mathrm{d} \gamma =0 \qquad\forall j. $$
nodes.statement_short: Same covering, partition of unity and b_j as in Theorem 3.3.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Reuse decomposition
nodes.statement: Then the argument leading to (\ref{aat}) shows that $$ f_0=\sum_j \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \,a_{jk} +\sum_j b_j \eta_j, $$ where the $a_{jk}$ are Gaussian atoms supported in $4B_j$ and $$ \sum_{j,k} \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le\,C\, \norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f_0}{L^1(\gamma)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Argument of Theorem 3.3 gives atoms plus sum b_j eta_j.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Remaining term
nodes.statement: It remains only to prove that $\sum_j b_j \eta_j$ is in $\huat {\gamma}$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains: sum b_j eta_j in H^1.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Subtract phi_0 multiples
nodes.statement: We write $g_j=b_j \eta_j$ and observe that \begin{equation} \int \sum_j g_j\,\mathrm{d}\gamma=0 \end{equation} because $f_0$ and the $a_{ij}$ have integrals zero. Thus $$ \sum_j g_j=\sum_j\Big(g_j-\int g_j\,\mathrm{d}\gamma \,\phi_0\Big), $$ where $\phi_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{trch}.
nodes.statement_short: Write sum g_j as sum (g_j - (int g_j) phi_0).
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Sup bound on g_j
nodes.statement: Since (\ref{1st}) remains valid for $f_0$, we have \begin{equation} \norm{g_j}{\infty}\le C\,\frac{1}{\gamma(B_j)} \int_{B_j}\mod{f_0}\,\mathrm{d} \gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sup bound on g_j from (3.10).
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{trch} thus applies to each $g_j$, and using also the bounded overlap of the $B_j$ we conclude \begin{align*} \norm{\sum_j g_j}{H^1(\gamma)}\,\le \, C\ \sum_j\big(1+\mod{c_{B_j}}^2\big)\ \int_{B_j} \mod{f_0}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma \,\le \, C\,\int \big(1+\mod{x}^2\big)\, \mod{f_0}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma. \end{align*} This concludes the proof of the sufficiency and the norm estimate.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 and bounded overlap bound the H^1 norm by int (1+|x|^2)|f_0|.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Necessity of M_loc condition
nodes.statement: The necessity of the condition $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} f\in L^1(\gamma)$ was obtained in Lemma \ref{necn}.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity of M_loc f in L^1 is Lemma 3.2.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: |x|^2 in BMO
nodes.statement: To prove the necessity of (\ref{nec}), let $0 \le f \in \huat{\gamma}$. We first observe that the function $x\mapsto \mod{x}^2$ is in $BMO(\gamma)$. Indeed, its oscillation on any admissible ball is bounded. Since $BMO(\gamma)$ is a lattice, the functions $g_k(x)=\min\set{\mod{x}^2,k}$ are in $BMO(\gamma)$, uniformly for $k \ge 1$.
nodes.statement_short: |x|^2 and its truncations lie in BMO(gamma) uniformly.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Duality
nodes.statement: By the monotone convergence theorem and the duality between $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$, $$ \int \mod{x}^2 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x)=\lim_k \int g_k(x) f(x)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x) \le C \norm{f}{\huat{\gamma}}. $$ The theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone convergence and H^1-BMO duality bound E_+(f).
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: State and defer claim
nodes.statement: We claim that the operator $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}}$ is bounded on $L^p(\gamma)$ for $1<p\le\infty$. Deferring momentarily the proof of this claim, we complete the proof of the corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Claim M_loc bounded on L^p; deferred.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: M_loc f integrable
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $f$ is in $L^p (\gamma)$. Then $\mathcal{M}_{	extnormal{loc}} f$ is in $L^1(\gamma)$, because $$ 
orm{\mathcal{M}_{	extnormal{loc}} f}{1}\le 
orm{\mathcal{M}_{	extnormal{loc}} f}{p}\, \le C 
orm{f}{p}<\infty, $$ since $\gamma(\mathbb{R}^n)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: M_loc f in L^1 since gamma is a probability measure.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: E_+ finite
nodes.statement: Moreover, $E_+(f)\le \norm{\mod{x}^2}{p'}\, \norm{f}{p} < \infty$, by H\"older's inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Holder gives E_+(f) finite.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 4.2 and duality
nodes.statement: Thus $f\in \huat{\gamma}$ by Theorem \ref{pos}. It also follows that the inclusion $L^p(\gamma)\subset \huat{\gamma}$ is continuous, and by duality we get the continuous inclusion $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$.

nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Reuse covering
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the claim. We shall use again the covering $\{B_j\}$ from the proof of Theorem \ref{char}.
nodes.statement_short: Use the covering B_j.

nodes.name: Local L^p bound
nodes.statement: First we observe that the inequality \begin{equation} \norm{\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} g}{p} \le C\norm{g}{p} \end{equation} holds when $\mathrm{supp}\, g \subset B_j$, with a constant $C$ independent of $j$. Indeed, $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}}$ is bounded on $L^p(\lambda)$, and $\mathcal{M}_{\textnormal{loc}} g$ is supported in the ball $4B_j$, where the Gaussian measure is essentially proportional to $d\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: M_loc bounded on L^p for functions supported in one B_j.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Sum over pieces
nodes.statement: Given a function $f \in L^p(\gamma)$, we write it as a sum $f = \sum f_j$ with $\mathrm{supp}\, f_j \subset B_j$ and with the sets $\{f_j \ne 0\}$ pairwise disjoint. We can then apply (\ref{eq:Lp}) to each $f_j$ and sum.
nodes.statement_short: Split f into disjointly supported pieces and sum.
